newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call ends down in volatile trade.
newsitem.headline: Indian call ends down in volatile trade.

text.p: Indian call rates ended the reporting Friday at 1.50-3.50 percent, off the day's opening levels of 7.50-8.50 percent in volatile trade, dealers said.
They said trades ranged between a high of 9.5 percent and a low of 0.5 percent on Friday.
Banks did not borrow from non-banking firms as this would increase their reserve requirements for the next fortnight, dealers said.

"Normally there is no borrowing on reporting days as this increases reserve requirements for the next fortnight," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "But with interbank borrowings now exempt from the 10 percent cash reserve ratio (CRR), there was action today."
The central bank announced in April that it had removed a 10 percent CRR on interbank liabilities.

"This prompted banks to borrow among themselves today," the dealer said. "But banks kept away from insurance companies, mutual funds and term lending financial institutions as borrowing from them would continue to attract CRR."
"These firms therefore found no takers today and went to the Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI) and the Securities Trading Corporation of India (STCI)," the dealer said.
DFHI and STCI borrowed from the non-banking firms and lent to banks, leading to a fall in call money rates, dealers said.
Trade in governement securities was on a dull note ahead of a five-year federal government bond auction, dealers said.
They said trades on the National Stock Exchange were worth 1.07 billion rupees against Wednesday's 2.75 billion.
The money market was largely inactive on Thursday as banks in the commercial capital of Bombay were shut for a local holiday.
The Reserve Bank of India auctions 30 billion rupee of federal government 5-year bonds on Friday.
Dealers said they expected the cut-off yield to be in the region of 12.60 percent.

The 13.50 percent government of India 1997 stock rose to 101.95 rupees from its last traded 101.60 rupees, the 13.12 percent 1999 to 102.70 rupees from 102.35 and the 13.05 percent to 100.60 rupees from 100.20 rupees, dealers said.
Treasury bills maturing in December 1997 yielded 8.90 percent against last yield of 9.25 percent, they said.
